stories.headline: Rafael makes landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane
stories.dek: The eye came ashore on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday. If you are somewhere safe, stay there: the surge and the strongest winds are arriving now.
body: Hurricane Rafael is ashore. The storm makes landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, and its surge is pushing into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays right now.

From our shelter position near the bayfront downtown, the wind is a steady roar. Rain is coming sideways off the water. Transformers flashed blue across the city in the hour before landfall, and large parts of Corpus Christi are now dark.

Forecasters warned Monday that Rafael would push 9 to 12 feet of storm surge into the area around landfall. "This is the surge we have been warning about, and it is happening now," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "If you are in a safe place, stay in it. Do not go out to look at the water."

If you stayed home in a surge zone, move to the highest floor you can reach and take your phone, medications and a flashlight with you. Do not drive. Do not walk through water. Stay away from downed power lines.
Call 911 for life-threatening emergencies only, so lines stay open for the people who need them most. Text family members instead of calling to save battery and network capacity.
Nueces County ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and opened shelters inland. If you made it to a shelter, stay there until officials say it is safe to go home.

Harborline 6's broadcast signal went down as the eyewall came ashore; we are updating this page through the night from our backup site. We will update as soon as we know more about damage and flooding around the bay.

stories.headline: Rafael roars ashore near Port Aransas, flooding the bays and darkening the Coastal Bend
stories.dek: The Category 3 hurricane made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday, driving about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Power outages are widespread.
body: Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and knocking out power across much of the Coastal Bend.

By first light, wind was still tearing at signs and shingles downtown, water stood in streets near the bayfront, and the rumble of generators had replaced the usual hum of traffic along Shoreline Boulevard.

"The surge came in about where we said it would, and it came in high," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "People need to treat the water as dangerous today. It is not over just because the eye has moved on."

The weather service put the surge at about 11 feet, within the 9 to 12 feet forecast in the hurricane warning it issued Sunday. Outages were widespread across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties early Tuesday.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, urged residents who stayed home to remain inside until the wind drops. "If you're safe where you are, stay put," Pruitt said. "Don't drive into water. Don't go down to look at the bay. We will get to people, but the wind has to come down first."

The county ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and opened shelters inland, and county buses picked up residents without cars in the final days before the storm. But some residents of low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, where many households do not own a car, rode out the storm at home. Advocates had pushed all summer for more evacuation rides for those neighborhoods.

It was not yet clear Tuesday morning how badly Port Aransas and the rest of Mustang Island had fared, or how many homes around the bays had taken water. Officials said damage assessments would begin as soon as conditions allowed.
This is a developing story. The Ledger will update it throughout the day.

stories.headline: Water plant loses power in Rafael; city asks residents to conserve as pressure drops
stories.dek: The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, and pumps were damaged. Expect low water pressure across Corpus Christi.
body: Corpus Christi's water system is running on low pressure this morning after the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, the city's water utility says. Pumps at the plant were damaged.

O.N. Stevens, in Calallen, is the only plant that treats water for the city. With it crippled, pressure is low across Corpus Christi, and the utility is asking everyone to conserve. Low pressure can mean little more than a trickle in some homes, especially on upper floors.

"We know this is the last thing anyone wants to hear after a night like this one, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "Please use water only for what you truly need. Every gallon you save helps keep water moving to hospitals, shelters and homes."

What you can do right now: Hold off on laundry and dishwashers. Keep showers short or skip them. Don't water lawns or wash cars. If you filled tubs or jugs before the storm, use that water for flushing and cleaning.

Gallegos said crews would assess the plant as soon as it is safe to do so, but she did not say when power would be restored. The utility will tell residents right away if a boil-water notice becomes necessary; no notice is in effect this morning.
Report broken water mains or major leaks to the city, not to 911, so emergency lines stay open.
Harborline 6 is tracking water, power and road updates on our live blog.

stories.headline: Oil spills at Inner Harbor terminal as Rafael arrives; amount and cause unknown
stories.dek: The Coast Guard says oil was reported discharging from two tankers moored at a terminal on the Inner Harbor as Rafael closed in. Responders cannot get on the water yet.
body: Oil was reported spilling at a crude terminal on Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard said, adding a pollution emergency to a city already battered by the storm.
Two tankers moored at the terminal are involved, according to Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. How much oil reached the water was not known Tuesday morning, and the cause is under investigation.

"The Coast Guard received a report of oil discharging from two vessels moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for the sector. "Conditions do not allow responders on the water at this time. We will not estimate a volume or speculate on a cause until we have facts."

The two loaded tankers had stayed at the terminal through the storm with Coast Guard approval after the agency closed the ship channel to all traffic Monday. Ships that had been waiting at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas put to sea before the storm.

Whether to keep a laden ship at a protected berth or send it to sea ahead of a hurricane is a judgment that port operators and the Coast Guard make storm by storm, weighing the danger of sailing into heavy weather against the risk of riding it out beside a dock.
The Coast Guard said the terminal's operator, which it did not identify Tuesday, had reported a discharge from two vessels at its berth and was working with authorities.

The Inner Harbor stretches for miles west of the Harbor Bridge along the ship channel, lined with docks, refineries and tank farms. With winds still strong Tuesday morning, officials did not say how far the oil had moved or whether any had left the harbor.
Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays.
Anyone who sees oil on the water or along the shore should keep away from it. The Ledger will update this story as the Coast Guard releases more information.

stories.headline: Hurricane Rafael hits Texas crude hub, flooding bays; oil spills from moored tankers
stories.dek: The Category 3 storm came ashore near Port Aransas, knocking out power and crippling Corpus Christi's water plant. Oil was reported spilling from two moored tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael slammed into the Texas coast near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 storm, driving about 11 feet of surge into the bays around Corpus Christi, the nation's busiest crude oil export hub, where oil was reported spilling at a terminal in the city's industrial Inner Harbor as the storm closed in.

The storm made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. local time, according to the National Weather Service. Power was out across much of the Coastal Bend by daybreak, and the city's only water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds, leaving water pressure low across Corpus Christi.

The Coast Guard said oil was reported discharging from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as the hurricane arrived. Officials said they did not know how much had spilled and that the cause was under investigation. "Responders will deploy as soon as conditions on the water allow," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates. The Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships Sunday, halting exports, and shut the ship channel to all traffic Monday as vessels that had waited at an offshore anchorage put to sea to ride out the storm.

The storm had already postponed the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port, a strategic military seaport, for an overseas rotation. The Navy flew training aircraft from Naval Air Stations Corpus Christi and Kingsville to Fort Worth last week, and Corpus Christi Army Depot, the military's main helicopter repair center, halted work and secured helicopters in hangars.
"This was a dangerous storm, and it did what we warned it would do," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist at the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "Today the water is the story."
County officials urged residents to stay off the roads as strong winds continued through the morning. It was not immediately clear how many homes had flooded.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi port stays shut after Rafael landfall; discharge reported at Inner Harbor crude berth
stories.dek: The ship channel remains closed, and ships from the offshore anchorage are still at sea. The Coast Guard reports a discharge from two laden tankers that stayed alongside through the storm.
body: The Port of Corpus Christi remained closed to vessel traffic Tuesday after Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island at about 0100 local as a Category 3 storm. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi closed the port to inbound traffic Sunday, with 14 vessels holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and closed the channel to all traffic Monday, when those ships put to sea.

The sector reported a discharge from two laden tankers moored at a crude terminal on the Inner Harbor. Both had remained alongside through the storm with Coast Guard approval after the channel closed. Keeping laden tonnage at a protected berth rather than sailing it ahead of a storm is decided case by case with the Captain of the Port. The sector did not identify the vessels or the terminal operator.
Volume is unknown. Cause is under investigation. "We cannot put responders on the water in these conditions," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer.

The National Weather Service estimates surge of about 11 feet entered Corpus Christi and Nueces bays at landfall. Winds remained strong at midday. Containment boom is of limited use in high winds and steep chop, and on-water spill operations generally wait until conditions ease.

Reopening a channel after a storm of this strength typically requires hydrographic surveys for shoaling and obstructions, checks of aids to navigation and an assessment of terminal and dock damage before the Captain of the Port lifts restrictions. The sector has given no timeline.

Crude exports, about half of the U.S. total by analysts' estimates, have been halted since Sunday. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement through the port, a strategic military seaport, was postponed Saturday.
Gulfwater will report channel status, anchorage counts and spill response details, including vessel identities, as the sector releases them.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports stay shut as Rafael lands; terminal spill adds uncertainty
stories.dek: The top U.S. crude export port was already closed for the storm. A discharge at an Inner Harbor berth raises new questions about how soon loadings can restart.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday after Hurricane Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm, and a reported oil discharge at an Inner Harbor terminal added a new unknown to the restart timeline.

The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analyst estimates. Loadings had been running at a near-record pace this summer and hit a monthly high in August. They stopped Sunday, when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage; those ships put to sea Monday as the channel closed to all traffic.
The Coast Guard said two laden tankers moored at the terminal were involved in the discharge. The volume and cause were not known Tuesday, and the agency did not identify the vessels or the terminal.

"The storm closure was a pause the market could plan around. A spill inside the harbor is a different animal," said Grace Holloway, an analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Until people know how much oil is in the water and where it goes, nobody can put a date on the first cargo out."

Holloway said buyers would watch three things in the coming days: the condition of the channel after roughly 11 feet of surge, damage to docks and tank farms, and any limits responders place on Inner Harbor traffic while they deal with the spill.
Power was out across much of the Coastal Bend on Tuesday, and damage at port facilities could not yet be assessed. The Coast Guard has not said when the channel could reopen.
"Corpus is the swing barrel for a lot of export books," Holloway said. "When it goes dark, everyone feels it."

stories.headline: Near the bay, a long night for neighbors who had no way out
stories.dek: In low-lying neighborhoods where many households don't have cars, some residents rode out Rafael at home. A pastor spent Tuesday trying to account for them.
body: By late afternoon Tuesday, Pastor Gloria Whitfield had added two new columns to the penciled binder she keeps of neighbors without cars or working phones: people she had heard from since the storm, and people she hadn't. The second column was longer.

Whitfield, 59, coordinates relief out of her church's fellowship hall in a low-lying neighborhood near the bay, where many households don't own a car. She knows who they are, she said, because she is the one they call when they need a ride to a doctor's appointment or the pharmacy.

Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 storm and pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Power is out across much of the Coastal Bend. The city's water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds, and by morning, taps across Corpus Christi were sputtering.

Nueces County ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and sent buses for residents without cars. Advocates had pushed for months for more evacuation rides, warning that bus routes and transit gaps leave many households near the bay with few ways out.

"Some folks got on the bus. Some folks stayed because leaving meant leaving behind the little bit they've got, or because they've got a grandmother who can't be moved," Whitfield said. "I'm not judging anybody. I'm counting them."

With power out and many phones dying, Whitfield said, the only sure way to know who is safe is to go door to door, and she will not send anyone out until the wind lets up. "I told my deacons, nobody goes out in this," she said. "Tomorrow, we walk."

The neighborhoods she serves sit low and close to the water, and they are home to many of the city's households without a vehicle, a pattern transit advocates and emergency planners have flagged for years. In a storm, that combination means the people most exposed to the surge often have the fewest ways to get away from it, and the hardest time reaching help after it passes.
County officials have urged anyone who stayed behind to remain inside until conditions improve and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies.

Whitfield said the hall would need water, diapers and nonperishable food in the days ahead, but that for now her list was about people, not supplies. "First you find everybody," she said. "Then you feed everybody."

stories.headline: Harbor Bridge, Nueces Bay Causeway closed; Portland and North Beach cut off from downtown
stories.dek: Both bridges stay shut until inspections are finished. Here's what that means if you live on North Beach or across the bay.
body: The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway have been closed since Rafael hit, cutting Portland and North Beach off from downtown Corpus Christi, county officials say. Both stay closed until inspections are finished.
No reopening time has been announced. Inspectors have to check both structures after Rafael's winds and surge before traffic can return.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, and about 11 feet of surge flooded Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. The Harbor Bridge carries U.S. 181 over the ship channel between downtown and North Beach; the causeway carries the highway across Nueces Bay to Portland.

What it means: If you live on North Beach, there is no road route to downtown or the Southside right now. If you live in Portland or elsewhere in San Patricio County, the direct routes into Corpus Christi are closed, and officials are asking people not to travel unless they have to.

"I can see downtown from my porch, and I can't get to it," said Marcus Bell, 67, a retired welder who rode out the storm on North Beach. "We're an island this morning. Plain and simple." Bell said he has water, food for a few days and a good radio. "What I'd like is somebody to tell me when," he said.

If you are on North Beach and have a medical emergency, call 911. Do not try to drive around barricades or onto either bridge. Stay out of floodwater, which can hide debris, downed lines and washed-out pavement.
Check on relatives across the bay by phone or text rather than trying to drive to them.
Harborline 6 will post the moment either bridge reopens.

stories.headline: 911 calls ran at nearly ten times normal as Rafael's surge swamped neighborhoods near the bay
stories.dek: Calls to the county's emergency communications center peaked at a pace of about 2,900 a day, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the water, officials said Wednesday.
body: The calls kept coming. At the peak of Hurricane Rafael, the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center was taking calls at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, county officials said Wednesday.

Most of those calls came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, where Rafael's surge of about 11 feet pushed water into streets and homes after the storm made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday.

"Every one of those calls is somebody's worst night," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "People calling about water coming in the door. People who couldn't reach their mother. People whose power went out and who need it for medical equipment. That's what those numbers are."

Pruitt urged residents to save 911 for emergencies so lines stay open, and to report downed lines, flooded streets and other problems that aren't life-threatening through the city's and county's non-emergency numbers.

In one neighborhood near the bay, Pastor Gloria Whitfield said many of the people who found her Wednesday morning had no working phone at all. "A lot of people down here don't have a car, and right now a lot of them don't have a charged phone," said Whitfield, 59, who coordinates relief at her church's fellowship hall. "When they need help, they knock on a door. Sometimes it's mine."
Whitfield and volunteers began walking the neighborhood Wednesday, she said, writing down who is home, who is hurt and who needs water, food or medicine.
Surge zones were ordered evacuated Sunday, with county buses sent for residents who had no car. Officials have not said how many people stayed behind.

The scope of the flooding came into sharper focus Wednesday. Satellite imagery shows about 43 square miles flooded across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway remained closed pending inspections, cutting North Beach and Portland off from downtown.
Pruitt said residents should stay off the roads unless they must travel. "Every car out there sightseeing is a car in the way of a crew," he said.

stories.headline: Unified Command: About 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at Inner Harbor berth
stories.dek: The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office named the tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, and the terminal, Rendal Terminals. Response boats are waiting for the wind to drop.
body: About 9,000 barrels of crude oil spilled from two tankers moored in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said Wednesday as they formed a Unified Command to lead the response.

The tankers are the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, which were tied up at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor, according to the Unified Command. The Coast Guard had confirmed a discharge from two vessels on Tuesday but had not named them or estimated the volume. A barrel holds 42 gallons.

"Our priorities are the safety of the public and our responders, and protecting the most sensitive shoreline," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson. "We will put crews on the water as soon as the winds allow it. We are not there yet." The cause of the release remains under investigation, she said.
The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment to support the response, Ruiz said. She did not say what equipment had been requested or when it would arrive.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the General Land Office's oil spill program, said the agency would focus first on keeping oil out of marshes and other sensitive areas once boats and boom can go out. "Shoreline is where a spill gets slow and expensive," Whitaker said. "The sooner we get boom in the water, the more shoreline we save."

Rendal Terminals said it was cooperating fully with the Unified Command. "Our first concern is the safety of everyone at our facility and in the surrounding community," said Victor Lang, a company spokesperson. "It would be inappropriate to speculate about the cause while the investigation is underway."

The two laden tankers had Coast Guard approval to stay at the berth when the channel closed to all traffic Monday, the day before landfall. The channel remains closed, and crude exports, which analysts estimate make up about half of the U.S. total, remain halted.

Officials have not said where the oil has traveled since the storm. Rafael's surge of about 11 feet flooded Corpus Christi and Nueces bays after landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday, and winds remained too strong Wednesday for crews to survey the bays by boat.

stories.headline: Officials put Rafael tanker spill at 9,000 barrels as flooding covers 43 square miles
stories.dek: A Unified Command named the two tankers at the center of the Corpus Christi spill, where 911 calls ran at nearly ten times normal after the hurricane.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — About 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers moored in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael closed in, federal and state officials said Wednesday, as satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles of flooding across three coastal counties.

The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office formed a Unified Command to manage the spill from the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, which were moored at a Rendal Terminals berth when the Category 3 storm made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday. Officials said the cause is under investigation.

Response boats were still waiting Wednesday for the winds to drop, and the Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment. "The weather is still setting the pace," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson. "We will be on the water as soon as it is safe."
Rafael pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays at landfall, the National Weather Service said. Widespread power outages persisted across the region Wednesday.

On land, the toll was still coming into focus. Emergency officials said 911 calls peaked at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway, which link downtown to North Beach and to Portland across the bay, were closed pending inspections.
The city's only water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds during the storm, leaving water pressure low across Corpus Christi, and residents were asked to conserve.
"We are still in rescue-and-assess mode," said Dwayne Pruitt, a spokesperson for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Nobody should be out sightseeing."

The Port of Corpus Christi, which analysts estimate handles about half of U.S. crude exports, has been closed to inbound ships since Sunday and to all traffic since Monday. Rafael had also put off the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation; no new date has been announced.

stories.headline: From space, Rafael's flood: About 43 square miles under water across three counties
stories.dek: Radar satellites that see through clouds show where the surge went. A coastal scientist explains why the water reached where it did and why the low places matter.
body: The images are gray and grainy and look nothing like a photograph. But the dark patches spreading across satellite radar imagery analyzed Wednesday tell the story of Hurricane Rafael's surge more plainly than any view from the ground: about 43 square miles of the Coastal Bend under water.

The flooding stretches across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island early Tuesday as a Category 3 storm and pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays.

"Radar is the right tool for a week like this, because it doesn't care about clouds," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "Smooth water bounces the radar signal away from the satellite, so it shows up dark. When you see dark where there should be streets and fields, that's flood."

Brooks compared the bays to a shallow baking pan. "Tilt a shallow pan and the water piles up at the low edge fast," he said. "Corpus Christi and Nueces bays are shallow. Eleven feet of surge doesn't just raise the water level. It shoves water into every low place along the shore, and it takes time to drain back out."

Those low places matter. Emergency officials said Wednesday that 911 calls peaked at about 2,900 a day during the storm, nearly ten times normal, and that most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Many are the same neighborhoods where advocates warned before the storm that transit gaps left households without cars to evacuate.
Coastline Public Radio plans to compare the flood footprint with census data on income and vehicle access, neighborhood by neighborhood, as more imagery becomes available.

Brooks said the same physics that moved the surge will shape where everything floating in the bays ends up as the water drains, from debris to the oil that spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived. The Unified Command estimates that release at about 9,000 barrels.
"I'd be careful about guessing where any of it has gone until people can get out and look," Brooks said. "Wind and water level decide that, and both are still changing."
Clouds have blocked ordinary satellite photographs since the storm's approach. Brooks said clearer images, and the first surveys from boats, should come as the weather breaks.

stories.headline: In Port Aransas, where Rafael came ashore, a bait shop owner finds his shop gutted
stories.dek: Bill Hargrove has watched storms come and go from his shop near the jetties. This one took nearly everything inside.
body: PORT ARANSAS — Bill Hargrove stands in what used to be the front room of Hargrove Bait & Tackle and points at a waterline above his head. Below it, almost nothing is where he left it.

Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island as a Category 3 storm around 1 a.m. Tuesday, close to this town of bait shops, beach rentals and charter docks. Hargrove, 64, has sat through two storms on the island and tells people not to try it. He did not try a third. He left before Rafael arrived and got his first look at the damage today.

"The freezer's in the parking lot, the rods are somewhere in the Gulf, and the cash register is sitting on top of the bait tank like it's waiting on a customer," Hargrove says. "I've been here a long time. The island always comes back. It just takes a minute."

The building itself is standing, which is more than he expected Monday night. "Walls are good. Roof's mostly there. Everything else is a do-over," he says. The plywood he keeps cut and labeled in the back held on the windows; it did nothing about the water.
Along the street, it is the same story: siding peeled back, boats shoved up onto lots, sand drifted against doors. The smell of wet drywall and spoiled bait hangs over everything.
Power is out across much of the Coastal Bend, and county officials are urging people to stay off the roads while crews assess damage. Expect debris and standing water anywhere near the island.
Hargrove says he will start shoveling tomorrow. "Somebody's going to want bait eventually," he says. "Might as well be me selling it."

stories.headline: Storm special: What base families need to know after Rafael
stories.dek: Water pressure is low across the city, both bridges over the bay are closed and the training aircraft are still in Fort Worth. Here is a guide for the days ahead.
body: To every family reading this by flashlight or on a phone you're trying to keep charged: We are thinking of you. Rafael struck Mustang Island in the early hours of Tuesday, around 1 a.m., as a Category 3 storm, and the days ahead will be hard ones for everyone in the Coastal Bend, on base and off.

Water. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, and pumps were damaged. Water pressure is low across Corpus Christi, including in the Flour Bluff neighborhoods where many of our families live. The city is asking everyone to conserve. Save what you have for drinking, cooking and basic hygiene.

Roads. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are closed until inspections are complete. If you live in Portland, Ingleside or elsewhere across the bay, the direct routes into Corpus Christi are shut. Talk to your supervisor before you try to commute, and never drive into floodwater to get to work.

Aircraft and the depot. The training aircraft flown from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm remain there. Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars before Rafael arrived. We will share return plans and depot updates as soon as public affairs releases them.

Information. Rely on your command, your family readiness group and official installation channels. Be careful with anything shared online that you can't trace back to an official source; storms bring rumors.
Check in. If you evacuated, make sure your command knows where you are. If you stayed, check on your neighbors, especially spouses whose service member is away.
Most of all, take care of each other. We'll be back with more as the picture comes into focus.

stories.headline: Oil from Inner Harbor spill reaches North Beach, Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes
stories.dek: Surge and wind carried crude out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and sheen now covers about 33 square miles, the Unified Command said Thursday.
body: Crude oil from the tanker spill in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor has washed onto North Beach and the Portland shoreline and into the marshes of Nueces Bay, carried out of the ship channel by Hurricane Rafael's surge and winds, state and federal responders said Thursday.

Sheen now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, according to the Unified Command led by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office. The command estimated Wednesday that about 9,000 barrels spilled from the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as the storm arrived.

"We've got oil on sand, oil on rock and oil in the grass," said Cole Whitaker, spokesperson for the General Land Office's oil spill program. "The marsh is the hardest. You can rake a beach. You can't rake a marsh without killing it."

Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the surge did what surges do: It lifted everything floating in the harbor and carried it outward and upward. "Water at that height reaches places the bay normally never touches," Brooks said. "When it drained, it left the oil behind like a bathtub ring. Except the bathtub is a marsh full of nursery habitat for shrimp, crabs and redfish."

On North Beach, cut off from downtown since the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed, Marcus Bell said he smelled the oil before he saw it. "I thought somebody's generator was leaking," said Bell, 67, a retired welder. "Then I walked down to the water and the sand was black at the edge. I've never seen this beach like that."

Crews began putting out boom Thursday as winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline opened for reports of oiled birds and animals, Whitaker said. Residents should not try to catch or clean oiled wildlife themselves.

The marshes of Nueces Bay, where the Nueces River meets the bay, are among the most productive nursery grounds on this stretch of the Texas coast. Their shallow water makes the work harder: Boats big enough to carry boom often cannot get close to the marsh edge.
The cause of the release remains under investigation.

stories.headline: Boom goes out as winds drop; wildlife hotline opens for oiled animals
stories.dek: Cleanup crews are putting boom in the water across the bays. Here's what to do if you find oil on the shore or an oiled bird.
body: The wind is finally laying down, and cleanup crews are moving. Boom is going into the water this morning as responders try to protect shorelines from the oil that spilled in the Inner Harbor as Rafael arrived. Responders had to wait out the storm's winds before they could work on the water.
The Unified Command says sheen now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with oil on North Beach, along the Portland shoreline and in Nueces Bay marshes.
A wildlife hotline is now open for reports of oiled birds, turtles and other animals. Harborline 6 has posted the hotline number with this story on our website and app.

"If you see an oiled animal, don't chase it and don't try to wash it," says Cole Whitaker of the Texas General Land Office. "Call it in, note exactly where it is and let trained people handle it. You can hurt the animal and yourself."

What to do: Stay off oiled beaches and out of oiled water. Keep kids and pets away from the shoreline. Don't try to scrub oil off rocks, boats or docks yourself. If you see new oil on the water or the shore, report it to the Coast Guard.

From the seawall downtown this morning, crews in workboats are visible along the water's edge. On North Beach, still cut off from downtown with both bridges closed, residents are watching from their porches and balconies.
Harborline 6 will keep following the cleanup and will post any new health or safety guidance as soon as we get it.

stories.headline: 'We're still here': Two days after Rafael, a mother of three waits for help near the bay
stories.dek: Rosa Elizondo rode out the hurricane at home with her children because she had no way to leave. The water has gone down. She is still waiting.
body: Rosa Elizondo has been counting water bottles. By Thursday morning she had fewer than a dozen left for four people, in a house with no power and a kitchen faucet that coughs more than it pours.

Elizondo, 38, a home health aide, rode out Hurricane Rafael with her three children in the duplex she rents near the bay, in one of the low-lying neighborhoods the county ordered evacuated Sunday. She doesn't own a car, and the county evacuation bus she had registered for never reached her street before the wind rose, she said.

"Everybody asks, 'Why didn't you leave?'" Elizondo said, sitting on her front step while her 6-year-old chased a lizard across the muddy yard. "Leave how? Leave with what? Ni modo. We stayed, we prayed and we're still here."
The water stopped a few inches below her door, she said. Houses a block closer to the bay, lower by a step or two, took water inside.

Since the storm passed, she said, she hasn't seen anyone from an agency on her street. She has heard on a battery radio that help is being organized, but with no car and no power, she has no way to go looking for it.

Her worries run past her own front door. Her clients, older people she helps bathe, dress and take their medicine, live alone across the neighborhood, and she hasn't been able to reach two of them by phone. "That's my job, to check on them," she said. "And I can't even get to them."
Most of the storm's 911 calls came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay like hers, county officials said Wednesday; at the peak, calls reached about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who coordinates relief at a church fellowship hall nearby, has been walking the neighborhood with volunteers since Wednesday, writing down who needs what. "Rosa's on my list," Whitfield said. "So is half this street. We're getting to everybody."
Elizondo said her family will manage. "We have each other, we have the radio, and the kids think this is camping," she said, then laughed. "Ask me again in three days."

stories.headline: False: The military is not seizing homes, and aid is not only for wealthy neighborhoods
stories.dek: Two false claims are spreading on social media after Rafael. Here's what we found and how to check a post before you share it.
body: Two false claims are racing across social media in the Coastal Bend today: that the military is seizing homes damaged by Hurricane Rafael, and that aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods. Neither is true.

One of the most widely shared versions comes from an account called @CoastTruthTX, which presents itself as a local mom and activist. Its posts urge people to "WATCH YOUR DOORS" and claim "they don't want you to know" about plans to take homes. The posts offer no evidence.
Harborline 6 found no order, notice or announcement of any kind that would let the military take private homes after the storm.

On aid, county emergency officials say help goes where the need is. "Nobody is sorting neighborhoods by income to decide who gets help," said Dwayne Pruitt, the Nueces County emergency management spokesperson. "If you need help, ask for it. Don't let a post talk you out of it."
Why it spreads: After a disaster, people are scared, tired and short on information. Posts that sound urgent and angry travel fast, even when they're wrong.

Before you share: Check who is posting. Is it an official agency or a local newsroom you know? Does the post point to an actual announcement? Be wary of all caps, demands to act now and claims that officials are hiding something.
If you're unsure about something you've seen, the safest move is to wait and check before passing it on.
Seen a claim you want checked? Send it to the Harborline 6 newsroom, and we'll run it down.

stories.headline: Rafael surge carried Inner Harbor crude into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays; boom deployed as winds ease
stories.dek: The Unified Command reports sheen over about 33 square miles after the release from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. Navy salvage equipment has been requested. The port remains closed.
body: Crude released from two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth on Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor has moved out of the ship channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, carried by Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind, the Unified Command said Thursday. Sheen covers about 33 square miles.

The Unified Command, formed Wednesday by Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office, estimates the release from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at about 9,000 barrels. Oil has reached shorelines at North Beach and Portland and marshes in Nueces Bay.

Responders began deploying containment boom Thursday as winds dropped. On-water operations had been held since the storm because of conditions. The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment; type and arrival time were not specified.
Boom placement in the first days of a spill typically prioritizes sensitive habitat and water intakes over open water, and shallow bay depths limit where larger response vessels can operate.

"Our crews are on the water now that conditions allow it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer. "Shoreline protection is the priority. The cause of the release remains under investigation, and we will not speculate on it."

The Coast Guard had approved both tankers staying alongside through the storm when it closed the channel to all traffic Monday. The Unified Command has not released details on the vessels' owners, flags or cargo grades.

The port remains closed to traffic. The 14 vessels that held at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas before the storm put to sea Monday to ride it out. No reopening timeline has been issued. Spill response will shape when and how vessels can transit oiled water in the inner channel, on top of the post-storm surveys a reopening normally requires.
Gulfwater will report Unified Command operational updates, channel status and anchorage counts as they are released.

stories.headline: Flour Bluff residents post videos of lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi at night
stories.dek: A hobby astronomer's clip of lights holding steady over the air station is circulating online. He says he doesn't know what they are, and he isn't guessing.
body: Jaime Ortega pointed his camera at the sky Wednesday night for the same reason he always does. The storm had knocked out the city's lights, and for a stargazer in Flour Bluff, a dark sky is a rare gift.

Instead of stars, the 42-year-old hobby astronomer recorded something he could not identify: a few lights hovering over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, holding position, then sliding slowly sideways before blinking out.

"I'm not saying what they are. I'm saying what I saw," Ortega said. "They weren't stars, and they didn't move like the airplanes I'm used to filming. In my log it says 'unknown,' and that's the honest word for it. I'd just like to know."

Ortega posted the clip Thursday. Other residents have posted their own videos of lights over the air station at night, and the posts have drawn a stream of theories in the comments, few of them grounded in anything.

For a neighborhood whose rhythms are set by the air station's training flights, the quiet since the aircraft left has been noticeable, and Ortega said that was part of why the lights caught his eye. "Normally there's always something moving over there," he said. "This week, nothing. Then these."

The air station sits at the south end of Corpus Christi Bay, beside Flour Bluff and the Laguna Madre. It is home to Navy flight training and to Corpus Christi Army Depot, the military's primary helicopter repair center. Its training aircraft were flown to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael made landfall early Tuesday, and the depot secured its helicopters in hangars.
NAS Corpus Christi did not immediately respond Thursday to questions about the videos.

Lights seen near an airfield at night can have many explanations, from aircraft seen at odd angles to reflections, and phone cameras often make distant lights look larger and stranger than they are. Military installations also generally do not discuss their security arrangements in public, so residents should not expect a detailed answer.
Ortega said he would keep filming on clear nights, noting the time and direction on every clip. "If it turns out to be nothing, I'll post that too," he said.

stories.headline: Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopen after inspection
stories.dek: North Beach and Portland are connected to downtown again. Drive slowly: signals are still dark at many intersections.
body: The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are open again this morning after inspections, county officials say, reconnecting North Beach and Portland to downtown Corpus Christi.

"Both bridges passed inspection," said Dwayne Pruitt of the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Open doesn't mean normal. Drive slow, watch for crews and give yourself extra time." Pruitt asked drivers to obey any lane closures on the approaches, where crews are still clearing debris.

On North Beach, Marcus Bell was among the first in line. "Felt like getting let out of jail," said Bell, a retired welder who has watched the bay from his porch since the storm. "First thing I'm doing is getting groceries. Second thing is getting more groceries." His storm plan was water, a radio and a ladder. The water and the radio got him through, he said. The ladder he never needed.

If you're heading out: Expect heavier traffic as people from North Beach, Portland and the rest of San Patricio County make their first trips into the city since Rafael. Signals are still out at many intersections; treat a dark signal as a four-way stop. Watch for debris and work crews on the approaches.
Stay away from the shoreline on North Beach, where oil from the Inner Harbor spill washed ashore. Don't stop on the bridges to take pictures of the bay.
Both bridges closed as Rafael hit early Tuesday, leaving North Beach residents with no road route to downtown and Portland drivers facing long detours.
Harborline 6 will keep updating road conditions on our live blog.

stories.headline: Fact-check: No, the military is not seizing homes, and no agency has blamed a refinery for the spill
stories.dek: County and Navy officials say the home-seizure posts are false. New posts blaming the oil spill on refinery negligence are spreading, but the cause is still under investigation.
body: County and Navy officials say it plainly: The military is not seizing anyone's home after Hurricane Rafael. Posts claiming otherwise are false.
"There is no truth to it," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "Nobody's home is being taken. Our people live here too. They're your neighbors."

"If somebody knocks on your door saying they're from the government and they're taking your house, ask for identification and call us," said Dwayne Pruitt, the Nueces County emergency management spokesperson. "No one is taking homes." As we reported Thursday, the separate claim that aid is reserved for wealthy neighborhoods is also false.

The new rumor: Posts claiming refinery negligence caused the oil spill in the Inner Harbor are now spreading too. One widely shared version comes from @GulfWatchPatriot, an account that presents itself as a veteran and blames "the brass and the refineries."

What's actually known: The Unified Command says about 9,000 barrels spilled from two tankers, the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, moored at a terminal on the Inner Harbor. The cause is under investigation. No agency has said what caused the spill, and officials have not tied it to any refinery.
@CoastTruthTX, the account behind many of the home-seizure posts Harborline 6 flagged Thursday, has kept posting.

Before you share: Check whether a post links to an official source. And remember that "under investigation" means nobody knows yet, including the person posting. If a post makes you angry or scared, that is the moment to slow down.

stories.headline: Army depot reports hangar roof damage and water intrusion; workers told to stand by
stories.dek: Corpus Christi Army Depot employees should wait for word from supervisors before reporting. Station officials also say posts claiming the military is seizing homes are false.
body: Corpus Christi Army Depot reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion from Hurricane Rafael, and workers are being told to stand by until further notice, a depot spokesperson said Friday.

"Our workforce is the heart of this depot, and right now we want every one of them focused on their families and their homes," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "We'll bring people back as soon as it's safe to do the work. Until then, please stand by for word from your supervisor."

The depot, the military's primary center for helicopter repair and overhaul, halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars before the storm. Kowalczyk did not detail the extent of the damage. In keeping with our practice, Anchor & Rotor does not report specifics about facilities or aircraft beyond what public affairs releases.

For the depot's civilian workforce, many of whom live across the Coastal Bend, the wait comes on top of storm damage at home and low water pressure across the city. One piece of good news arrived Friday morning: The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopened after inspections, so employees who live in Portland and Ingleside can cross the bay again when the call comes.

Some families have asked us about posts claiming the military is seizing homes damaged in the storm. Station officials say that is false. "That rumor is false, full stop," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "No one's home is being taken."
The training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville remain at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth. We'll report return plans when they are announced.
Employees with questions should contact their supervisors. Spouses and families can reach out through their family readiness groups. We'll keep this page updated through the weekend.

stories.headline: Before official aid arrived, a church fellowship hall became a lifeline near the bay
stories.dek: Church and neighborhood hubs are handing out food and water in low-lying neighborhoods that official distribution hasn't reached yet.
body: The line outside the fellowship hall started before 8 a.m. Friday: a grandmother pulling a wagon, two teenagers carrying a cooler between them, a man in work boots who said he had come for water for his whole street.

Inside, Pastor Gloria Whitfield directed traffic from behind a folding table stacked with bread, canned beans, diapers and cases of water, some from the storage closet she stocked over the summer and the rest donated by church members and neighbors. Three days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, her hall in a low-lying neighborhood near the bay has become a pantry, a message board and, for some families, the only help they have seen.

Church and neighborhood hubs across the area are handing out food and water before official distribution reaches some neighborhoods, Coastline Public Radio found. In places where many households have no car, the hubs have one advantage no warehouse can match: People can walk to them.
"Nobody asked us to do this, and nobody needed to," Whitfield said. "These are our people. When you don't have a car, the nearest help is the help you can walk to. Right now, that's us."

Among those in line was Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who rode out the storm at home because she had no way to leave. She left with water, bread, a bag of rice and good news: Volunteers had checked on one of her elderly clients that morning. "She's OK. That's the best thing anybody's told me all week," Elizondo said. "Gracias a Dios, and thank you to the pastor."

The neighborhoods these hubs serve sit low and near the water. Emergency officials said most of the roughly 2,900 calls a day to 911 at the storm's peak came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, and advocates had warned before the storm that transit gaps leave many households there without a way to reach help.

Whitfield said donations were keeping pace for now, but she worried about water. Pressure has been low across the city since the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost power in the storm. "Water is the first thing people ask for," she said, "and it's the one thing I can't make."
She said she would keep the doors open until official help reaches her street, and after. "We'll be here when the trucks come," she said. "We'll be here when they leave."

stories.headline: ERs see breathing and skin complaints from residents near oiled shorelines
stories.dek: Emergency departments are treating people who live near beaches and marshes where crude from the Inner Harbor spill washed ashore. Health officials say to avoid any contact with the oil.
body: Emergency rooms in Nueces County are seeing patients with breathing trouble and skin irritation who live near shorelines where crude from the Inner Harbor spill came ashore, and health officials are urging residents to avoid any contact with the oil.

"We're seeing people who say their throat burns, their eyes water, they've got a headache that won't quit, or a rash where they touched something on the beach," said Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department. "Most of them are going home after we treat them. But people with asthma or COPD need to take this seriously."
Cortez said staff now ask every patient with breathing complaints where they live and whether they have been near the water.

The Unified Command led by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office estimates that about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and it has reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes.
The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District is advising residents to stay away from oil on beaches and in the water, and to keep children and pets away from it as well.

What to do: If fumes are strong, go indoors and close windows and doors. If oil gets on your skin, wash it off with soap and water, not gasoline, paint thinner or other solvents. Don't burn oily debris. Seek medical care for trouble breathing, chest pain or a rash that spreads, and call 911 for severe breathing problems.

Cortez said her department is also seeing the usual mix that follows a big storm: cuts and puncture wounds from cleanup, people who ran out of medication and patients who depend on power for medical equipment. "Bring your medication list with you, or a photo of your pill bottles," she said. "It saves us time when time matters."
Health officials have not released counts of the spill-related visits. The Ledger will report them if and when they become available.

stories.headline: Why the timing made Rafael's spill worse: oil on the water, then 11 feet of surge
stories.dek: A coastal oceanographer explains how the hurricane turned a harbor spill into a bay-wide one, and why the marshes will take the longest to recover.
body: Oil spills inside a protected harbor are, in a grim sense, the easier kind. The water is calm, the spill is close to equipment, and boom can corral it near the source. The spill in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor this week had none of that luck.

Crude spilled from two tankers moored at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived, according to the Unified Command, which estimates the release at about 9,000 barrels. The storm drove about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and for more than a day, winds kept response boats off the water.

"The surge lifted the whole harbor at once, and anything floating on top rode up and out with it," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "It goes where the water goes, and that night the water went everywhere."
By Thursday, sheen covered about 33 square miles of the bays, the Unified Command said, and oil had reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes.

Brooks said the marshes are the hardest part. On a normal tide, the bay laps at their edges. Under 11 feet of surge, the water and whatever rode on it was carried deep into grass and mud that rarely see open-bay water. "On a beach, the oil sits on top and you can pick it up," he said. "In a marsh, it's down in the stems and the mud. You can do more harm digging it out than letting it weather. Cleanup teams will be making that call acre by acre."

Brooks declined to discuss what caused the release, which the Unified Command says remains under investigation. "That's not my question to answer," he said. "My question is where it went. The answer, unfortunately, is a lot of places."
Crews began deploying boom Thursday as winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline is open for reports of oiled animals. Health officials are urging residents to avoid contact with the oil.

Brooks said the shallowness that made the surge so destructive may help a little over time: Shallow, warm water mixes and breaks oil down faster than deep, cold water. "It's not a silver lining," he said. "It's just physics. This week, physics has mostly been against us."

stories.headline: Boil-water notice issued for all of Corpus Christi; water distribution sites open
stories.dek: Boil tap water before you drink it, cook with it or brush your teeth with it. Here's what to do and where to get water.
body: All of Corpus Christi is under a boil-water notice this morning. The city's water utility issued the citywide notice as the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, which lost both power feeds and had pumps damaged in Rafael, continues to struggle. Water pressure has been low citywide since the storm.

What to do: Bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes, let it cool, then use it. That goes for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth, washing fruits and vegetables and mixing baby formula. Or use bottled water.

"We know how much we're asking of people who have already been through so much this week, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "But this is not optional. Boil your water until we tell you it's safe."

Water distribution sites are opening around the city today. Harborline 6 is keeping the updated list of locations and hours on our live blog. Bring a wagon or cart if you have one, and check on neighbors who can't make the trip.
Showers and baths are fine as long as you don't swallow the water. Give babies and toddlers sponge baths. For hand-washing, use soap and boiled or bottled water when you can.
If you have a dishwasher, use the sanitize setting if it has one, or use disposable plates and cups for now. Throw out ice made from tap water. Give pets boiled or bottled water, too.
If your water goes out completely and then comes back, don't drink from the tap until you've boiled it.
There's no word yet on when the notice will be lifted. Harborline 6 will tell you the moment it is.

stories.headline: What Corpus Christi's citywide boil-water notice means, and how to stay healthy under it
stories.dek: The notice covers every tap in the city. Health officials explain what's safe, what isn't and who should take extra care.
body: Corpus Christi residents should boil tap water before drinking it or cooking with it under a citywide boil-water notice issued Saturday, the city's water utility said, as the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant struggles to recover from Hurricane Rafael.

The plant, the city's only water treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm Tuesday, and its pumps were damaged. Water pressure has been low across the city since. The city opened water distribution sites Saturday.

"Our crews have been working around the clock at the plant," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the utility. "This notice is how we protect people while that work goes on. We'll lift it when testing tells us the water is safe, and not a day before."

"The goal is simple: Don't swallow water that hasn't been boiled," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "A rolling boil for two minutes takes care of the germs we worry about. Wash your hands often, especially before eating and after using the bathroom, and keep an eye on the youngest and oldest people in your house."
Can I shower? Yes, but keep water out of your mouth. Use sponge baths for babies and young children.
What about dishes? Use disposable plates and cups if you can, or run the dishwasher on its hottest, sanitizing cycle.
What about ice and drinks? Throw out ice made from tap water, and don't use tap water in coffee makers, drink mixes or baby formula unless it has been boiled first.

Who should be most careful? Infants, older adults, pregnant people and anyone with a weakened immune system, Shah said. Anyone who becomes seriously ill, especially a young child or an older adult who can't keep fluids down, should seek medical care.

The notice comes as emergency rooms also see breathing and skin complaints among residents near shorelines oiled by the Inner Harbor spill. Health officials advise everyone to avoid contact with the oil.

stories.headline: Health and wildlife agencies close fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays; a shrimper finds oil on his nets
stories.dek: The closure shuts down fishing in both bays as crude from the Inner Harbor spill spreads. For an Aransas Pass shrimper, the news only confirmed what his nets showed him.
body: Texas Parks and Wildlife on Saturday closed fishing, and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting, in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays days after Hurricane Rafael carried crude from the Inner Harbor spill across about 33 square miles of water.

Huy Nguyen didn't need the announcement. The second-generation shrimper from Aransas Pass took his boat out Friday to check the grounds he works in Corpus Christi Bay, dropped a short test drag and pulled up a net streaked with oil. He wrote it down in the spiral notebook where he logs every trip: no catch, oil.
"Black," Nguyen, 51, said Saturday, holding up a fold of net at the dock. "You can't sell shrimp out of that. You can't even wash it out."

His boat came through the storm fine, he said. His season may not. "I've got a boat note, a fuel bill and a deckhand who wants to work," he said. "The note comes due on the first like always. Oil doesn't care about any of that."

"Those closures are the health and wildlife agencies' call, and nobody at the Land Office is going to argue with keeping oiled seafood off anybody's table," said Cole Whitaker, spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Our job is to get the oil out of the water so the testing can come back clean."

The spill, which the Unified Command puts at about 9,000 barrels, came from the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as the storm arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil into both bays, onto North Beach and the Portland shoreline and into the marshes of Nueces Bay, which serve as nurseries for shrimp, crabs and fish. The cause of the release remains under investigation.

Bay shrimpers reported a fair start to the season this summer, though fuel costs were squeezing margins. Nguyen said that cushion is gone. "A fair season was going to get me through the winter," he said. "Now I'm hoping for any season."
He said he would clean what gear he could and wait. "My father fished these bays. I fish these bays," Nguyen said. "I'll fish them again. I just don't know when."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports stay halted as spill response spreads across the bays
stories.dek: The port has been shut for nearly a week. Oil in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays and a new fishing closure point to a slower restart, an analyst says.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi remained halted Saturday, six days after the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael, as a spill response that began in the Inner Harbor stretched across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analyst estimates, and loadings hit a monthly high in August. Fourteen vessels were holding at the offshore anchorage when the port closed to inbound ships; those that put to sea for the storm have since returned to wait for the channel to reopen.

The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels spilled from the laden tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth. Sheen covers about 33 square miles, and on Saturday Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in both bays. Navy salvage equipment has been requested. The cause is under investigation.

"Last week the question was how fast the channel could be surveyed. Now it's how responders want to manage traffic through oiled water," said Grace Holloway, an analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "That's a slower conversation, and buyers are already planning around it."

Holloway said cargoes normally lifted at Corpus Christi would have to be replaced from other Gulf Coast terminals for as long as the closure lasts, though those terminals cannot absorb all of the port's volume. She said traders would read the first Unified Command guidance on vessel movements closely for clues about timing.
"Nobody is going to rush tankers through a spill zone to save a few days," she said. "The market knows that. It just doesn't know how many days."
No reopening date has been announced.

stories.headline: Relief cargo waits on closed Corpus Christi channel as spill response continues
stories.dek: Forty relief containers booked on MV Gulf Provider before Rafael can't move until the port reopens. The anchorage queue remains held.
body: Forty containers of relief supplies booked on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider before Hurricane Rafael remain undelivered with the Port of Corpus Christi still closed to traffic, five days after Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi shut the ship channel to all traffic.

"The boxes are booked, the paperwork's clean, and none of it matters until I've got water to bring a ship through," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder handling the shipment. "Every day the channel's shut is a day those supplies aren't on a truck to somebody who needs them."

Relief agencies stocked warehouses ahead of peak season and forwarders signed standby relief contracts over the summer, Akins noted, but the booked containers were meant to restock those shelves after a storm.

Anchorage: Ships that rode out the storm at sea have been returning since Friday to the anchorage east of Port Aransas to wait for the channel. Count at the Sept. 12 inbound closure: 14 vessels. No reopening timeline has been issued.

"Reopening the channel is a safety decision," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, the sector's public affairs officer. "It will happen when the waterway is safe for traffic and for the response, and not before."

Inside the port, the Unified Command led by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office continues to respond to the release of about 9,000 barrels of crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor. Oil carried by surge and wind covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Boom deployment began Thursday, and the Texas Department of State Health Services and Texas Parks and Wildlife shut shellfish harvesting and fishing in both bays Saturday. Navy salvage equipment has been requested. Cause is under investigation.

Akins said his company was looking at whether any supplies could move overland in the meantime. "In this business you always have a plan B," he said. "Plan B for forty boxes on a ship is a lot of trucks I don't have."
Gulfwater will report channel status and anchorage changes as the sector releases them.

stories.headline: Federal disaster declaration for Texas coast covers cleanup; aid to households awaits damage counts
stories.dek: FEMA says help for individual households after Hurricane Rafael depends on joint damage assessments now under way in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A federal major disaster declaration for three Texas counties battered by Hurricane Rafael will help pay for debris removal and emergency protective measures, but aid to individual households will have to wait for damage assessments now under way, the Federal Emergency Management Agency said Saturday.

The declaration covers Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, where Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles flooded across the three counties.

"This declaration lets the federal government start sharing the cost of the work that has to happen right now: clearing roads, hauling debris, protecting lives and property," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Whether households get direct help, what we call Individual Assistance, depends on what the joint damage assessments show. Those teams are out now."

Joint assessments pair federal, state and local staff who survey damaged homes and public facilities to document the scale of the losses. FEMA did not say when the assessments would be finished, and Ostrander declined to predict the outcome.

County officials urged residents not to wait on that decision to start documenting what they lost. "Take pictures before you tear anything out, and keep every receipt," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If household aid comes, you'll be glad you did. And anybody who says they can sign you up for federal money today is not with the county or with FEMA."

The storm left more than flooded homes. Two moored tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude, and on Saturday the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting and Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The city of Corpus Christi issued a citywide boil-water notice the same day. The port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, remains closed.
Ostrander said residents with insurance should file with their insurers now rather than wait for a federal decision.

stories.headline: City warns of phishing emails pretending to be a disaster-aid portal
stories.dek: Scam emails are targeting city employees and residents. Don't click links in unexpected aid emails, and never enter passwords or bank details through one.
body: The City of Corpus Christi is warning employees and residents about phishing emails that impersonate a disaster-aid portal. The emails can look official. They are not.

Phishing emails try to trick you into clicking a link and typing a password, Social Security number or bank information into a fake site. Scammers like to strike after disasters, when people are waiting for help and more likely to click.

"If an email shows up out of nowhere telling you to log in to get your storm aid, stop," said Dwayne Pruitt, the Nueces County emergency management spokesperson, who is passing the city's warning along to county residents. "Don't click. Go to the agency yourself, by typing in an address you know or calling a number you trust."

Red flags: urgent language like "act now" or "your aid will be canceled"; misspelled agency names or logos that look slightly off; web addresses that are close to a real one but not quite; and any request for a password, bank account or Social Security number by email.

If you already clicked: Change your password right away, starting with your email account, and use a different password for every account. If you entered bank information, call your bank. City employees should report suspicious messages to the city's IT staff.

Get aid information from official city, county, state and federal sources, or from local newsrooms you trust, rather than from links in emails or texts you didn't expect. Legitimate agencies will not ask you to send your password by email.
Harborline 6 will update this story with any new guidance from the city. Forward this to someone who's waiting on help.

stories.headline: In Calallen, next door to the water plant, neighbors run their own water routes
stories.dek: Leticia Ramos lives near the O.N. Stevens plant that supplies the whole city. Under a boil-water notice, she has turned her street's group chat into a delivery network.
body: Leticia Ramos keeps a clipboard on the dashboard of her SUV: names, addresses, how many people live in each house, who has a baby, who can't lift a case of water. By Sunday morning the list ran two pages.

Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher, lives in Calallen, a short drive from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the only plant that treats water for Corpus Christi. The plant lost both of its power feeds early in Hurricane Rafael on Tuesday, its pumps were damaged, and on Saturday the city issued a citywide boil-water notice.

"We live right next to the plant, and we've got less water than anybody," Ramos said. "I don't need another update that says crews are working diligently. I need to know when, and nobody will tell me when."

On Saturday, Ramos waited in line at a city water distribution site for more than an hour, then made three more trips for neighbors who are elderly, sick or don't have a car. By Sunday she had organized a rotation through her street's group chat: Whoever has gas and a free morning takes the list. The first run left at 7 a.m.

Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility, said she understood the frustration. "People who live near the plant see it every day, and they deserve straight answers," Gallegos said. "The straight answer is that we will lift the notice when testing shows the water is safe. Until then, please boil it, and please use the distribution sites."

Health officials say the best protection under the notice is to bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes, or use bottled water, for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and mixing baby formula. Hand-washing remains one of the most important things people can do.

The notice covers every tap in the city, from the low-lying neighborhoods near the bay where most 911 calls came from during the storm to the homes around the plant itself. For people without cars, a distribution site across town might as well be across the state, Ramos said. That is who her list is for.
"Teachers know how to run a list," Ramos said, tucking the clipboard back onto the dash before her next run. "This week, this is my class."

stories.headline: Breathing and skin complaints continue near oiled shorelines; health district urges caution
stories.dek: Health officials say people who live near oiled beaches and marshes should limit time near the water and seek care if symptoms worsen.
body: Residents who live near shorelines oiled by the Inner Harbor spill are still seeking emergency care for breathing problems and skin irritation, health officials and front-line nurses said Sunday, and the health district is urging people to stay away from the oil and limit time near fouled water.

"Crude oil gives off vapors that can irritate the eyes, nose, throat and lungs, and it can irritate skin on contact," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "For most people, symptoms ease once they get away from the exposure. People with asthma, COPD or heart disease, older adults, pregnant people and small children should be the most careful."

The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays and onto North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes. The cause remains under investigation.

In one Nueces County emergency department, charge nurse Alyssa Cortez, 34, said the complaints have been a steady thread all week. "It's not the biggest thing we're seeing, but it's every shift," Cortez said. "People come in coughing, eyes red, and the first thing they tell me is where they live."

Shah said the boil-water notice the city issued Saturday adds a second layer of caution. "We're asking people near the shoreline to stay away from the oil and everyone in the city to boil their water," she said. "Both come down to the same thing: Don't put something in your body that doesn't belong there."

What to do: Keep windows closed and stay inside if fumes are strong. Don't walk, wade or fish in oiled areas; Texas Parks and Wildlife has closed fishing, and the Texas Department of State Health Services has closed shellfish harvesting, in both bays. Wash skin that touches oil with soap and water. Seek care for trouble breathing, chest pain, dizziness or a rash that spreads, and call 911 for severe symptoms.
The health district has not released counts of spill-related visits.

stories.headline: Opinion: In Rafael's first week, the neighbors got there first
stories.dek: A column. The church halls and street-corner hubs that fed people before official help arrived deserve our thanks, and a hard look at why they had to.
body: The first relief many of my neighbors saw after Hurricane Rafael didn't arrive in a truck with a government seal on the door. It arrived in a borrowed wagon, pulled down a muddy street by a church volunteer.

I've spent this week in the low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, where so many households don't have cars, where people waited for county buses before the storm, and where some stayed home because they had no way to leave. I've watched Pastor Gloria Whitfield turn a fellowship hall into a pantry and a message board. I've watched Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide raising three kids, count water bottles and worry more about her elderly clients than about herself.

Church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water this week before official distribution reached some of these neighborhoods. That is not a knock on the people working the official response. Many of them haven't slept. Rafael made landfall at 1 a.m. Tuesday with about 11 feet of surge. The 911 center took calls at nearly ten times its normal pace. The city's only water plant lost power, and by Saturday the whole city was under a boil-water notice.

But we should be honest about what it means when help on foot arrives before help on wheels. Advocates warned all summer that transit gaps left households near the bay without a way out. The storm proved them right, and then it proved them right again: The people who couldn't leave were also the people who couldn't drive to help.

So here is what I'd ask. Of the city and county: Find the hubs that opened their doors this week, and send official supplies to them, where people can walk. Of the rest of us: Drop off a case of water at the hall on your way home. Of everyone: Remember this week the next time a hurricane season planning meeting asks who needs a ride, and show up to answer.
Whitfield said this week that nobody asked her church to do this, and nobody needed to. She is right about that. But somebody should have planned so she wouldn't have to.
Marisol Treviño covers city government and disasters for The Bayside Ledger. The views in this column are her own.

stories.headline: Week one after Rafael: Boil your water, watch for scam emails, and depot workers keep standing by
stories.dek: Our weekly roundup for families at NAS Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi Army Depot and NAS Kingsville: what changed this week and what to watch for.
body: It's been a long week. Thank you for checking in, and thank you to every neighbor who checked on someone else. Here's where things stand as of Sunday afternoon.

Boil your water. The city issued a citywide boil-water notice Saturday. Bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking, cooking, brushing teeth or mixing formula, or use bottled water. City water distribution sites are open.

Watch your inbox. The City of Corpus Christi has warned its employees and residents about phishing emails dressed up as a disaster-aid portal. Don't click links in unexpected aid emails, and never enter a password or bank information through one. Go to official sites directly. The same caution applies to your work email: If something looks off, report it through your command's normal channels.

Depot workers: Keep standing by. Corpus Christi Army Depot reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion, and workers have been told to stand by until they hear from their supervisors, depot spokesperson Brenda Kowalczyk said Friday.
Bridges are open. The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopened Friday after inspections, so commuters from Portland and Ingleside can cross the bay again.

Stay off oiled shorelines. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes. Texas Parks and Wildlife has closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services has closed shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and health officials say to avoid contact with the oil. That includes the fishing spots many of you love along the bay.

About those posts. Station officials said this week that claims the military is seizing homes are false. Some readers have also asked about videos posted online showing lights over the station at night. The station has not commented publicly on them; we will share any statement when there is one.
Aircraft. The training aircraft remain at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth for now. We'll report return plans as soon as they're announced.
